newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen poet seeks power in predecessor's name.
newsitem.headline: Chechen poet seeks power in predecessor's name.

text.p: Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev's campaign posters show him and late president Dzhokhar Dudayev, whose name is almost as revered in Chechnya as Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin's was under communist rule in the Soviet Union.
Yandarbiyev, the acting Chechen president, is trying to fend off 15 challengers to keep his job in the Monday's election in the rebel region.
He served as Dudayev's vice-president, which meant he automatically took the reins of power when the fiery general was reported killed in a Russian rocket attack in 1996.
Despite this, many observers say Yandarbiyev has the poorest chances of winning of the four top contenders.
Although all the main candidates have invoked Dudayev's name, it is the cornerstone of Yandarbiyev's campaign.
"If Dzhokhar were alive today, I think he would vote for Yandarbiyev," he told Reuters in an interview.

Zelimkhan Adbul-Muslimovich Yandarbiyev was born in 1952 in Kazakhstan, where the entire Chechen population had been deported eight years earlier by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin, who said they might conspire with Hitler's invading armies.
Yanadarbiyev returned to Chechnya with his family after Stalin died.
Before becoming one of Chechnya's best known poets, he worked as a mason, shepherd and oil-well driller.

He ran foul of Soviet authorities at an early age, helping to form a literary association called "Pkharmat" (Prometei) with other young Chechen writers and poets. It was shut down by the KGB for alleged nationalist tendencies in 1979.

He helped form the Vainakh Democratic Party in 1989 which later helped overthrow Chechnya's communist-installed overlords and began its recent history of confrontation with Moscow. At the time Dudayev was still a general in the Soviet air force.
Yet despite being one of the first Chechens to oppose Russian control openly, he was not one of the prominent figures during most of the 1994-96 war.
"He wasn't one of the big political or military heroes in the war. This has weakened his position greatly," said Professor Aslan Dukayev of the Chechen State University.
Yandarbiyev's entourage seems almost fatalistic about his fate and he began intensive campaigning late.

"The president awaits the results impassively. If the people decide he should be president then it means the almighty Allah has decided it should be so. If not, he has a different path for him," said his campaign press secretary.
Yandarbiyev has played on his adherence to Islamic principles in his campaign and takes credit for establishing Koran-based Shariat courts which have recently come into use.
